newsitem.title: JAPAN: Wall Street fall drags Tokyo stocks along.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street fall drags Tokyo stocks along.

text.p: Tokyo shares tumbled in fast-paced trading on Friday, spooked by a sharp drop on Wall Street overnight.

The stock market fall triggered some morning losses in Japanese government bonds, but they later recovered and there was no major spill-over effect for the dollar, which remained steady at around 113.10 yen and 1.5470 marks, slightly stronger than its overnight levels.
The Nikkei average of 225 leading shares quickly fell more than 500 points, or 2.5 percent, in hectic morning trade, the first time it has fallen below the key level of 20,000 in three months.
After recovering some ground, the market then resumed its slide in the afternoon session.
With one hour of trading left at 2 p.m. (0500 GMT) the key Nikkei index was off 468.06 points at 20,033.14, a loss of 2.28 percent.
Traders said the New York fall meant that the vital flow of foreign investment into Tokyo stocks may dry up.
"Due to the New York sell-off, we can't hope for foreign investors' buying in Tokyo. That dampened the Nikkei average," said Harushige Kobayashi, deputy general manager at Yamaichi Securities Co Ltd.
The Nikkei last sank below the 20,000 level on September 3 this year, when it marked an intraday low of 19,920.02.

New York blue-chip shares fell nearly 100 points or 1.54 percent on Thursday after a late burst of computerised programme selling in what was a roller-coaster session. This was the Dow's biggest point loss since mid-July and followed a 71-point drop on Wednesday.
The outlook for Friday's opening on Wall Street was also less than rosy.

In trading on the Globex automated system, the key Standard & Poor's 500 futures contract was down nearly seven points at 727.50. Analysts calculate that the loss would equal about a 60-point drop in the Dow Jones industrial average.
Stock markets around the globe have been nervous since Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan talked about the possibility of equity markets moving too high.
Speaking a week ago, the head of the U.S. central bank said that "irrational exuberance" could be affecting the markets.
World markets were also unsettled this week by fears that Japanese investors may be turning away from U.S. Treasuries, which would push up U.S. interest rates and hurt Wall Street stock prices.

The stock market fall dragged down Japanese government bonds (JGB) in early trading but the market later recovered in what analysts said was a flight to quality in the safety of government-backed securities.
The key March contract for 10-year JGBs was off just 0.04 points at 124.85.
Currency traders, meanwhile, said they saw little or no impact from the Nikkei drop.
